title: Given an array of positive numbers and a target, count how many contiguous subarrays have a product strictly less than the target. (LeetCode: Subarray Product Less Than K)
shortTitle: Subarrays with Product Less than a Target (Sliding Window)
keyPoints: Use a sliding window: expand right to multiply in, shrink left to divide out when the product reaches or exceeds the target.
At each right position, the count of valid subarrays ending there equals the current window length (right - left + 1).
The technique works because all numbers are positive, so the product changes monotonically as the window grows and shrinks.
Each pointer only moves forward, so the total time is O(n) with O(1) space.
If the target is 1 or less, no subarray of positive integers can have a product below it, so the answer is zero.
Guard the shrinking loop so that left never passes right.
This technique breaks if zeros or negatives are present because the product is no longer monotonic.

s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window on the right, shrink on the left when the product reaches the target, and add the window length at each step to count valid subarrays.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sliding window** – maintain a window `[left, right]` with a running product; expand `right` to include new elements and shrink `left` when the product reaches or exceeds the target.
- **Counting** – at each valid right position, the number of valid subarrays ending at `right` is `right - left + 1`.
- **Monotonic product** – because all elements are positive, multiplying grows the product and dividing shrinks it, which is the property the window needs.
- **Shrink guard** – never let `left` pass `right`; check `left <= right` in the shrink loop.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space; each pointer moves forward at most n times total.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India tracks daily growth multipliers for a portfolio. He needs to count how many consecutive stretches of days have a combined growth factor below a risk threshold. He grows a window by including the next day on the right; if the combined factor gets too big, he drops days off the left until it is safe again. For each new right day, every valid window ending there counts.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly below a target is a sliding-window problem that works beautifully because all the numbers are positive. Positivity gives a monotonic property: multiplying a new element into the product can only make it larger, and dividing an element out can only make it smaller, which is exactly what a sliding window needs to decide when to expand and when to shrink.

The counting trick is that at each right position, after shrinking from the left to bring the product back below the target, every subarray ending at right and starting anywhere from left to right is valid. The count of those subarrays is simply the window length, right minus left plus one. Because each pointer only moves forward, the entire algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, the portfolio risk team tracks daily growth multipliers and needs to count how many consecutive stretches of days have a combined growth factor below a risk threshold. Over long histories the brute-force check of every stretch would be quadratic, and the single sliding window gives the exact count efficiently.

The senior-level point is the positivity requirement. This technique depends on every number being strictly positive so the product changes monotonically as the window grows and shrinks. If zeros or negatives were allowed, the shrink-from-left logic would break. The target <= 1 edge case must also be guarded, because no product of positive integers can fall below 1, and using `long` for the product avoids overflow when the window grows large before the shrink fires.

Remember one sentence: expand right to multiply in, shrink left to divide out, and add the window length at each step to count valid subarrays in O(n) time.
